strengths: Clear empirical demonstration of an important practical problem: fixed hyperparameters underperform across tasks with different privacy/compute budgets, with compelling visualization (Figure 1)

Novel theoretical contribution (Theorem 5.1) providing MSE-based analysis of optimal clipping that explains why empirical findings contradict prior theory, particularly counterintuitive benefits of larger C under tight privacy

Insightful mechanistic analysis including gradient re-weighting perspective (Section 5.3) showing how clipping disproportionately affects harder classes, supported by gradient norm distribution analysis (Figure 3)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple privacy levels (ε ∈ {0.25,...,8}), model architectures (ViT-Base, ViT-Tiny, ResNet-50), and datasets with varying characteristics, with systematic hyperparameter grids
Well-reasoned explanation for why common practices fail: automatic clipping underperforms in hard settings (Figure 5), and fixed-steps batch size guidance doesn't apply to fixed-epoch setting
Rigorous empirical methodology with proper privacy accounting (PRV), merged validation sets, multiple seeds, and thorough appendices documenting additional analyses
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only image classification with ViT-based fine-tuning (FiLM), small-to-medium datasets (≤87k examples). No evidence findings extend to NLP/LLMs, federated learning, full-model training, or other domains—limiting relevance to modern DP learning

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 5.1 analyzes MSE for single minibatches, not multi-step training dynamics; ignores minibatch sampling noise; provides no closed-form formula for practitioners to compute C* directly. Theory motivates the phenomenon but offers limited actionable guidance beyond 'C depends on gradients'

Limited practical utility of main contributions: core finding that hyperparameters must be tuned per-task is unsurprising; paper uses exhaustive grid search (hundreds of runs) but proposes no efficient tuning algorithm. Cumulative noise rule (σ√T) is presented as improvement but remains somewhat ad-hoc with heuristic components (minimum steps threshold)

Batch size guidance lacks theoretical foundation: minimum steps requirement identified empirically but not theoretically justified; rule requires knowing N and epochs upfront (circular for practitioners); sensitivity to this threshold not thoroughly analyzed

Limited algorithmic novelty: paper is primarily diagnostic (explaining why methods fail) rather than constructive (proposing solutions). No new optimization methods, tuning strategies, or algorithms provided

Experimental rigor concerns: only 3-5 random seeds with wide error bars; macro accuracy focus may obscure whether improvements concentrate on already-easy classes; 'best hyperparameters' selection criteria not fully specified; no statistical significance testing

Presentation issues: dense paper with key results scattered across appendices; 'learning problem difficulty' is an intuitive but informal organizing principle; some notation introduced but inconsistently used

Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned; LLM usage in code generation (though validated); some implementation details relegated to appendices; fixed-epoch constraint is somewhat artificial and may not generalize to fixed-steps DP literature

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic empirical investigation with extensive experiments across multiple datasets, models, and privacy levels
Addresses a genuine practical problem: the common but suboptimal practice of fixing C and B across different tasks
Clear problem motivation and effective visualizations (e.g., Figure 1) demonstrating the core issue
Useful intuitive explanations through gradient re-weighting perspective and per-class analysis
Detailed experimental setup and hyperparameter grids supporting reproducibility
Novel characterization of optimal clipping via Theorem 5.1 based on MSE minimization
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core finding that hyperparameters should vary with problem difficulty is unsurprising and lacks novelty beyond standard hyperparameter tuning

Weak theory-practice connection: Theorem 5.1 minimizes MSE for fixed minibatches, not training loss; doesn't rigorously explain why larger C helps under tight privacy or resolve contradiction with Koloskova et al. (2023)
Narrow experimental scope restricted to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (FiLM) on image classification; unclear if findings generalize to full model fine-tuning, other domains, or other DP algorithms
Insufficient baseline comparisons: only compares to automatic clipping; missing comparisons with Bayesian optimization, adaptive clipping, and other tuning approaches
Lack of actionable framework: no clear decision rules for practitioners; 'problem difficulty' not quantified; how to determine minimum steps for batch size remains unclear
Batch size analysis introduces cumulative noise σ√T heuristic without theoretical justification for why this metric should work
Small sample sizes for some experiments (3-5 seeds); no significance testing or confidence intervals; no sensitivity analysis for δ
Missing investigation of computational cost of hyperparameter tuning and how many runs practitioners need

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: Demonstrates that fixing C and B across tasks is suboptimal with convincing evidence (Figure 1) relevant to practitioners
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Multiple datasets, models, privacy levels, with exhaustive grid search and proper experimental methodology
Surprising and well-demonstrated finding: Shows larger C is optimal under tight privacy (contradicting prior theory), consistently replicated across settings
Novel theoretical insight: Theorem 5.1 provides MSE-optimal clipping dependent on gradient distributions, a new perspective complementing prior work
Multi-faceted mechanistic analysis: Explains findings through gradient norm distribution shifts (Figure 3) and clipping-as-reweighting interpretation (Figure 4)
Practical guidance for batch size: Proposes cumulative DP noise σ√T heuristic that improves over prior fixed-steps approaches
Clear presentation: Well-structured paper with excellent visualizations that effectively communicate findings
weaknesses: Limited scope significantly constrains impact: Only image classification with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (FiLM); full-model tuning generalization unvalidated; only DP-Adam in depth; short training horizons (8-32 epochs)

Theory-practice gap in Theorem 5.1: Minimizes single-step MSE but doesn't rigorously connect to multi-step optimization; doesn't directly explain why larger C helps under tight privacy (explained via empirical gradient shifts instead); practical predictive value unvalidated

Incomplete characterization of batch size guidance: Cumulative noise rule σ√T lacks theoretical justification; minimum steps requirement is dataset-dependent and uncharacterized; substantial scatter in Figure 7 with unreported prediction error

Limited actionable guidance: Shows C and B depend on problem difficulty but provides no formula or algorithm; practitioners still need exhaustive grid search; 'learning problem difficulty' informally defined and not quantifiable
Confounding factors in joint hyperparameter tuning: Learning rate jointly optimized with C and B; interactions not fully disentangled; authors note √B scaling but don't isolate contributions
Incomplete experimental comparisons: Only compares automatic clipping empirically; doesn't evaluate adaptive clipping or Ponomareva et al. batch size heuristics; limited baseline coverage

Fairness implications underdeveloped: Figure 4 shows small C severely harms hard classes with fairness implications, but paper neither quantifies fairness gaps nor proposes fairness-aware hyperparameter selection
Statistical analysis could be stronger: Reports min-max bands over 3-5 seeds rather than confidence intervals; no formal hypothesis tests; some reported differences small relative to variance
Missing ablations and sensitivity analysis: No direct comparison of benefit from tuning C vs. B; sensitivity to minimum steps threshold not explored; sequential vs. joint tuning not compared

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets, models, and training methods with extensive ablations and careful experimental design
Practical importance: demonstrates that fixed hyperparameters across tasks are systematically suboptimal and provides actionable guidance (Table 1)
Novel empirical insight that gradient norm distributions shift toward larger values under tighter privacy, explaining counterintuitive finding that larger C improves performance with smaller ε
Insightful analysis of clipping as gradient re-weighting with intuitive retained weight metric and per-class analysis showing differential impacts on easy vs. hard classes
Fixed-epoch batch size rule using cumulative DP noise (σ√T) is more principled than prior fixed-steps heuristics and better matches practical compute constraints
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-organized experiments including thorough appendices
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 5.2 (optimal clipping) is impractical since finding C* requires knowing actual gradient magnitudes; would need additional DP mechanisms. Theorem 5.4 is standard smoothness-based optimization analysis
Theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis uses standard DP-SGD but experiments use normalized variant; theory explains phenomena post-hoc rather than justifying practical guidance

Batch size rule incomplete: proposed combination of minimum steps with cumulative noise plateau is heuristic without theoretical justification; minimum step count varies by dataset (Fig. A35) without guidance on determining it on new domains

Limited scope despite breadth: main results focus on parameter-efficient fine-tuning (FiLM/LoRA with ~0.5-1.5% parameters); full fine-tuning shows qualitatively different behavior but relegated to appendix
Concept of 'learning problem difficulty' defined informally throughout; lacks formal quantification despite being central to the narrative

Experimental practicality concerns: exhaustive (C,B,η) grid search is computationally expensive; practitioners with tight budgets cannot replicate tuning; no cost-benefit analysis of when tuning justifies the expense
Gradient distribution shifts under DP observed empirically but not theoretically explained; unclear whether phenomenon is fundamental or specific to transfer learning setting
Incomplete ablations: paper claims joint tuning of (C,B,η) is crucial but doesn't isolate individual contributions of each parameter

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic empirical evaluation across multiple datasets, models, and training methods with extensive hyperparameter grids
Clear intuitive explanation of clipping as gradient re-weighting with effective per-class analysis (Figure 4) showing fairness implications
Practical contribution via cumulative noise framework (σ√T) for batch size selection under fixed-epoch training
Well-designed experiments demonstrating that fixed hyperparameters across tasks lead to suboptimal performance
Gradient distribution analysis effectively explains empirical findings of why optimal C increases under tight privacy
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: main finding (optimal hyperparameters vary with task difficulty) is incremental and intuitive; contribution is empirical characterization rather than fundamental insight

Theorem 5.2 has severe practical limitations: depends on knowing actual gradients (unusable during training), uses restrictive assumptions, and provides only post-hoc explanation without guiding hyperparameter selection
Theory-practice gap: analysis uses unnormalized DP-SGD but experiments use normalized DP-Adam; theory cannot be applied during actual optimization
Critical scope limitation insufficiently highlighted: findings focus on PEFT (FiLM with ~1% parameters) but full fine-tuning behaves fundamentally differently; generality unclear
Learning rate is re-tuned for every configuration, confounding effects and masking the true contribution of C and B tuning; no ablation separating joint vs. independent tuning
Insufficient practical guidance: Table 1 provides only qualitative rules (no quantitative guidance); practitioners must still run expensive grid searches, unclear advantage over existing heuristics
Limited mechanistic understanding: observes gradient distributions shift under tight privacy (Figure 3) but lacks deep explanation of why this occurs
Incomplete comparisons: limited baseline comparisons (only AUTO-S for alternatives), no Bayesian optimization discussion, adaptive clipping relegated to appendix
Statistical significance unclear: many differences appear small with only 3-5 seeds; no confidence intervals or significance tests provided
Batch size contribution feels incremental: σ√T is straightforward (total noise = noise per step × steps); minimum steps requirement is intuitive

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study across 10+ model-dataset combinations with multiple training paradigms (DP-SGD, DP-Adam; FiLM, LoRA, from-scratch, full fine-tune)
Clear practical relevance: demonstrates that common practice of fixing C and B across tasks is suboptimal, with actionable guidance (Table 1)
Strong visualization and presentation: Figures 1 and 4 effectively communicate the core phenomena and per-class gradient re-weighting insights
Theoretical contributions: Theorem 5.2 derives optimal clipping bound via MSE minimization, Theorem 5.4 connects to optimization progress, providing grounding for empirical observations
Gradient re-weighting perspective (Section 5.3) provides intuitive understanding of clipping as class-specific importance weighting
Reproducible research: public datasets, detailed hyperparameter grids, multiple seeds, extensive appendices support verification
Honest treatment of limitations: full fine-tuning exception (Section I.3) and edge cases discussed transparently
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: The insight that hyperparameters should vary with problem difficulty is relatively intuitive; that gradient distributions shift under different ε is expected. The core message ('tune jointly for each task') validates an expected phenomenon rather than revealing a surprising insight

Theoretical results lack practical utility: Theorem 5.2's optimal C* depends on unknown quantities (G_C*, N_C*) requiring private estimation; Assumption 5.1 (no mini-batch sampling noise) is unrealistic. Theorems provide formal grounding but don't enable practical application

Batch size guidance is heuristic: The σ√T metric is empirically motivated but lacks principled theoretical justification. The dataset-dependent minimum steps requirement (Figure A35) undermines generalizability

Critical limitation incompletely addressed: Full fine-tuning (Section I.3) shows the core easy-vs-hard pattern breaks down—both settings prefer very large C. This substantial exception raises questions about finding generality but is relegated to appendix

Limited practical efficiency: Proposed solution requires grid search over (C,B,η) for each task—no method for efficient hyperparameter discovery. Computational cost limits practical adoption versus fixed defaults

Scope limitations: Experiments focus on parameter-efficient fine-tuning (0.5-1.5% trainable), small models/datasets, only δ=10^-5, fixed-epoch constraint. Scalability to modern large-scale settings and other compute budgets unclear

Incomplete analysis of mechanisms: While paper documents that gradient norms shift with difficulty (Figure 3), it lacks deep insight into why specific aspects of 'difficulty' (privacy, backbone capability, data scarcity) affect this shift. Re-weighting perspective appears somewhat post-hoc
Statistical methodology: Only 3-5 random seeds (lower end of standard practice), min-max bands instead of confidence intervals, no formal significance testing

Limited comparison with alternatives: Automatic clipping comparison limited to one method (Section H). No systematic comparison with Bayesian optimization or other HPO approaches despite mentioning them in related work
